founded.what: The year an ancestor of the family settled at Urville and began to farm a vineyard there, by the house's own account.

place: Urville, Côte des Bar, the Aube, Champagne

kind.means: A négociant manipulant, a house in the trade's own word: a family that farms its own vines around Urville, buys grapes beyond them and makes the wine itself.

story: Drappier tells a long story at Urville, in the Côte des Bar of the Aube. Its cellars, by the house's account, were built in 1152 for the Cistercian abbey of Clairvaux, and the slope above the village was planted with vines by the monks. In 1808 an ancestor of the family settled at Urville and began to farm a vineyard there, the year the house dates itself from. In 1836, by the house's account, a fire ravaged Urville and left a thick cover of ash on a hillside, where the family found vines did well: the parcels took the name of the cinders, and a slip in the land register gave it its S. In the 1930s the family's grandfather replanted Pinot Noir at Urville, and neighbours mocked him for it, by several accounts. After the Second World War the family bought the old Cistercian cellars and put them to use. Charles de Gaulle (1890 to 1970), who lived at Colombey-les-Deux-Églises nearby, served the house's Champagne, and in 1990 the house named a cuvée for him. André Drappier (1926 to 2025) led the house for decades. It is a family house of Pinot Noir, made with very little sulphur.

style.line: Pinot Noir led and fruit driven, from the Kimmeridgian slopes of the Côte des Bar, made with very little sulphur and low dosage, and including a Brut Nature with no dosage at all.
style.grapes: Pinot Noir leads, from the family's vines around Urville in the Côte des Bar, with Chardonnay and some Meunier; Carte d'Or is about three quarters Pinot Noir, by the house's sheets.
style.reserve: Carte d'Or holds about two fifths reserve wines, by the house's English technical sheet.
style.malolactic: Grande Sendrée goes through its malolactic conversion, by the house's technical sheets for the 2012 and the 2015.
style.lees: Grande Sendrée ages about nine years in bottle in the house's cellars, by its sheets.
style.dosage: Low: Carte d'Or 5 to 7 grams a litre by the house's sheets in different languages, Grande Sendrée about 4, with a liqueur aged in wood.

nv.name: Carte d'Or Brut
nv.note: The non vintage Brut in the yellow label, introduced in 1952: about three quarters Pinot Noir with Chardonnay and Meunier, and about two fifths reserve wines.

cuvee.name: Grande Sendrée

first.what: Not settled: one merchant gives 1975 and a house letter speaks of an old 1974 bottle, so no first vintage is taught.

cuvee.rhythm: Made only in vintages the house chooses. Its own sheets show the 2010, 2012 and 2015, and merchants list the 2006, 2008 and 2009.
cuvee.blend: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, with Pinot Noir a little over half, by the house's sheets.
cuvee.sites: Grande Sendrée itself: an archipelago of plots on Kimmeridgian marl at Urville, in the Côte des Bar, covered in ash after the fire that ravaged the village in 1836, by the house.
cuvee.making: The first pressing alone, pressed very gently, then moved by gravity, settled naturally and taken through its malolactic conversion, with very little sulphur and no filtering, by the house. The wood moves by vintage: about a third of the wines aged in casks for the 2012, all of them for the 2015. The dosage is about 4 grams a litre, a liqueur aged fifteen years in wood.
cuvee.lees: About nine years in bottle in the house's cellars, by its sheets for the 2012 and the 2015.
cuvee.bottle: A bottle in the shape of the reign of Louis XV, an eighteenth century form, by the house's sheets.
cuvee.young: Pear, ripe peach and baked bread, with toasted almond, lemon peel and a touch of honey, by the importer's sheet and a critic's note on one vintage.
cuvee.aged: No note read follows a bottle over long years, so none is told here; the house's sheet called the 2015 ready to drink after eight years of maturing.

forms.name: Grande Sendrée Rosé
forms.note: The rosé of the same plots, about seven tenths Pinot Noir with Chardonnay in the 2018: strawberry, pomegranate and violet, by the house.

cuvee.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius, never ice cold; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass.

table.house45: Drappier is a family house of Urville, in the Côte des Bar, far south of Reims in the Aube. The family dates it from 1808, and its cellars were built for the monks of Clairvaux in the twelfth century. In the 1930s the family grandfather replanted Pinot Noir there while his neighbours laughed. Charles de Gaulle lived nearby and poured the house's Champagne at home. The style is Pinot Noir led, with very little sulphur and very little sugar added at the end. Most guests know Carte d'Or, in the yellow label. The prestige cuvée is Grande Sendrée, from a slope once covered in ash.
table.house10: Drappier is the Pinot Noir family house of Urville in the Côte des Bar, dated from 1808 and poured by Charles de Gaulle.
table.cuvee45: Grande Sendrée is the vintage prestige cuvée of Drappier, named for a slope at Urville. A fire burned the village in 1836 and left the hillside under ash, so the plots took the name of the cinders. It is Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, with a little more Pinot Noir. The wine is made with very little sulphur and ages about nine years in the cellar. Expect ripe peach, baked bread and toasted almond. It comes in a bottle shaped like those of the eighteenth century. I serve it at about nine degrees in a white wine glass.
table.sale: If you like a story in the glass, Grande Sendrée comes from a slope at Urville once covered in ash, Pinot Noir led and aged about nine years. Shall I open a bottle for the table?
table.cuvee10: Grande Sendrée is Drappier's vintage prestige cuvée, Pinot Noir and Chardonnay from a slope at Urville once covered in ash.
table.cuvee20: Grande Sendrée is the vintage wine of Drappier, from plots at Urville that a fire of 1836 covered in ash. It is Pinot Noir led, made with very little sulphur and aged about nine years.

guests.q: Why is Sendrée spelt with an S?
guests.a: The name comes from the cinders, cendres in French, left by the fire of 1836. By the house's account a slip in the land register gave the name its S, and the house kept it.
In the Côte des Bar, in the Aube, far south of Reims and nearer Chablis than Épernay. Its slopes share the Kimmeridgian soil of Chablis.

guests.q: Is the Charles de Gaulle cuvée the prestige wine?
guests.a: It is another of the house's fine cuvées, named for the general in 1990. The class sheet names Grande Sendrée as the house's prestige cuvée.

traps: The class sheet prints Grand Sendrée; the label reads Grande Sendrée, with an e, and Sendrée with an S, not a C.
The Côte des Bar is in the Aube, far south of Reims and nearer Chablis.
Brut Nature means no dosage at all, drier than Extra Brut.
Cuvée Charles de Gaulle is Drappier's tribute to the general, not the prestige cuvée the class sheet names.

sheet.label: Grande Sendrée
sheet.note: The sheet drops the e of Grande. The label reads Grande Sendrée, the great plot of cinders, spelt with an S by the house's own account of a slip in the land register.

questions.q: Which prestige cuvée on the class sheet comes from the Côte des Bar, from plots once covered in ash?
questions.exp: Grande Sendrée is Drappier's, of Urville in the Aube. Clos des Goisses is Philipponnat's walled vineyard at Mareuil-sur-Aÿ, Celebris is Gosset's and Grand Siècle is Laurent-Perrier's blend of several vintages.

questions.q: Which grape did the Drappier family replant at Urville in the 1930s, the grape that leads its wines?
questions.exp: Pinot Noir, which leads Carte d'Or at about three quarters and Grande Sendrée at a little over half. Arbane is one of the rare old grapes of the Aube, not the house's lead.

questions.q: After what event were the plots of Grande Sendrée named, by the house's account?
opts: A fire that covered the slope in ash
A flood that buried the vines in silt
A hailstorm that stripped the vines bare
A monk who planted the first vines there
questions.exp: A fire ravaged Urville in 1836 and left the hillside under ash, cendres in French, and the plots took the name. The Cistercian monks of Clairvaux belong to the story of the cellars, not of the name.

report: Built on the library's p-drappier and contradicting none of it: founded 1808, Urville in the Côte des Bar, Pinot Noir led, very little sulphur, Carte d'Or of 1952, the Brut Nature and the de Gaulle link.
The fire: the plan's why says 1838; the house's page and every sheet read say 1836, which the record follows.
cuvee.first is empty: one merchant gives 1975 and a house letter mentions an old 1974 bottle, and neither is confirmed; the library gives no year either.
The 1808 ancestor and the grandfather who replanted Pinot Noir are described, not named: their dates were not found in two sources, and the accounts differ on the grandfather's name.
André Drappier is named with his dates, 1926 to 2025, by the Drinks Business and the World of Fine Wine; the family members who lead the house since are living and never named.
The cellars of 1152 and the fire of 1836 rest on the house's own pages and are told as its account; the house's pages differ on when the cellars became a presbytery, which the record leaves out.
The dosage of the 2012 differs between two house papers, 4 and 4.5 grams a litre; the 2015 sheet gives 4.2, so the record says about 4.
The 2015 sheet gives nine years in bottle and also speaks of eight years of maturing; the record keeps about nine and quotes the eight in cuvee.aged.
style.vessels is empty: the house does not state the vessels of the range on any page read; the casks of Grande Sendrée are told in cuvee.making.
Carte d'Or's dosage differs between the house's sheets in different languages, 5 to 7 grams a litre, so the record gives the range.
kind.code: the letters NM were not read on a label; they are inferred from the house buying grapes beyond its own vines, which a refuter should confirm on a label.
The year 1990 for Cuvée Charles de Gaulle rests on merchants' accounts only and is said once, in a guest's answer and the story; a refuter should read it.
